chunks: And from him, from al-Nadr and Fadalah, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Hafs, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was in prayer, and next to him was al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him). The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said 'Allahu Akbar', but al-Husayn did not respond with the Takbir. Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said 'Allahu Akbar' again, but al-Husayn (peace be upon him) did not respond with the Takbir. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) continued to say 'Allahu Akbar' and al-Husayn (peace be upon him) continued to refrain from saying it, until he completed seven Takbirs. Then al-Husayn (peace be upon him) responded with the Takbir in the seventh one. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Thus it became a Sunnah.'

key_terms.التَّكْبِير: Saying 'Allahu Akbar' (God is the Greatest), a ritual utterance in prayer
key_terms.سَبْعَ تَكْبِيرَاتٍ: Seven Takbirs, referring to the specific number of times the Prophet said 'Allahu Akbar' in this narration
key_terms.سُنَّةً: A established prophetic tradition or legal precedent
key_terms.يُعَالِجُ: To persist or continue doing something, often implying a deliberate or sustained action

ai.seo_question: What is the origin of the practice of delaying the Takbir until the seventh time in Shia prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the origin of the Sunnah of delaying the Takbir in prayer, where Imam al-Husayn (peace be upon him) waited until the seventh Takbir before responding. This incident highlights the practical transmission of ritual nuances from the Prophet to the Imams, establishing a specific legal precedent for the timing of the Takbir that distinguishes Shia jurisprudence. It underscores the role of the Imams in preserving and clarifying the Prophet's silent or subtle practices that were not explicitly codified in the Quran.
